title: That Silver Coating on Your Mithai May Be Aluminium, and Doctors Say It Can Harm Your Liver
excerpt: Cheap aluminium foil is increasingly being substituted for genuine silver leaf on Indian sweets, with health experts warning of risks to the liver, kidneys, and nervous system from accumulated heavy metals.
body:
• Food safety tests across India have found that the silver-like coating on many sweets is actually aluminium foil, a cheaper substitute that can accumulate in body tissues, bones, and even the brain.
  • An ITRC Lucknow study of 178 silver leaf samples found that 17 were made entirely of aluminium sold as silver leaf, with nickel and lead levels exceeding prescribed safety limits.
  • Aluminium is classified as a neurotoxic metal; prolonged exposure through food can impair kidney and liver function, weaken bones by reducing calcium absorption, and contribute to digestive disorders.
  • FSSAI regulations require silver leaf to contain a minimum fineness of 999/1000 silver and ban the use of animal-origin materials in manufacturing, though enforcement remains inconsistent.

The gleaming silver coating on a piece of kaju barfi or a decorated paan may look appetizing, but doctors and food safety officials are warning that what passes for chandi varak — traditional silver leaf — on Indian sweets is increasingly likely to be aluminium foil, a toxic metal that accumulates in the body and can damage the liver, kidneys, and nervous system.

The issue has drawn fresh attention as health experts highlight the risks of consuming aluminium-adulterated sweets, particularly during festival seasons when demand for decorated mithai surges and cost-cutting substitutions become more common.

The Adulteration Problem

Genuine chandi varak is made from 99.9% pure silver, a metal that is biologically inert and harmless when consumed in the tiny quantities used for food decoration. Aluminium, however, is classified as a neurotoxic metal by health authorities. When sweets makers substitute aluminium foil for genuine silver leaf to cut costs — silver is significantly more expensive — consumers unknowingly ingest a hazardous substance.

A study by the Indian Toxicology Research Centre (ITRC) in Lucknow examined 178 silver leaf samples and found that 17 were made entirely of aluminium but sold as silver leaf. In these adulterated samples, nickel and lead concentrations exceeded the limits prescribed under India's Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules. An additional 81 samples contained silver content ranging from 82.5% to 99.8% — below the required 99.9% purity standard.

"Cheaper silver foil often contains toxic metals such as aluminium, lead and cadmium. The accumulation of these substances in the body can damage vital organs."

— Roshan Singh, District Collector, Ujjain

In Ujjain, District Collector Roshan Singh recently directed food safety officials to stop the use of silver foil on sweets entirely, citing health risks from toxic metals. The district's food safety department reported collecting 513 food samples in the 2025-2026 fiscal year, exceeding its target of 420.

What Aluminium Does to the Body

Unlike silver, aluminium is not biologically inert. When consumed through adulterated food coatings, the metal accumulates in body tissues because the digestive system cannot properly break it down or flush it out. According to medical experts and the National Environment Health Association, the health effects include damage to the liver and kidneys, which bear the burden of filtering toxins; reduced calcium absorption, leading to weakened bones; digestive problems including stomach infections, pain, and ulcers; and potential nervous system damage affecting memory and cognitive function over time.

Research published in the International Journal of Electrochemical Science found that aluminium leaches more readily into acidic and aqueous solutions and at higher temperatures — conditions that are relevant to many Indian sweets containing acidic ingredients or served warm.

How to Spot the Difference

Food safety experts recommend several simple tests. Genuine silver leaf, when rubbed between the palms, disappears completely; aluminium forms a small ball. When ignited, real silver melts into a tiny silver bead, while aluminium burns and leaves behind greyish-black ash. If wiped off a sweet, aluminium residue tends to stick to the fingers, while silver does not.

FSSAI regulations, amended in 2016, now require food-grade silver leaf to have a minimum fineness of 999 parts per 1,000 silver, a uniform thickness of up to 2.8 gm per square metre, and no use of animal-origin materials at any stage of manufacturing. The aluminium thickness limit is designed so that aluminium, which cannot be hammered as thin as silver, effectively fails to meet the standard.

Enforcement Gaps Remain

Despite the regulations, enforcement has been inconsistent across states. The Delhi High Court stayed the implementation of the 2016 FSSAI standards after traditional silver leaf manufacturers challenged the ban on animal-origin processing methods, in which silver is hammered inside ox intestines to achieve the required thinness. The legal challenge has left a regulatory grey area that benefits neither consumers nor compliant manufacturers.

As festival season approaches, doctors recommend buying sweets from established, FSSAI-licensed shops, checking for quality certifications, and performing basic tests at home before consuming foil-decorated sweets. The safest approach, health experts suggest, is to simply peel off the decorative foil before eating — whether it is genuine silver or adulterated aluminium, it adds no flavor or nutritional value to the sweet.
image_caption: Silver-coated Indian sweets. Regulators have found that some silver foil on mithai may actually be aluminium, which doctors warn can harm the liver.
